articles.headline: Certificate.
articles.text:
Certificate.

This certificate is drawn, signed and acknowledged by the parties hereto in order to conform to the requirements of the civil code of the territory of Dakota demanded of parties transacting business in said territory under a ficticious name, or under a designation not showing the names of the persons interested as partners in said business.

We the undersigned hereby certify that we have this day entered into copartnership under the name of the "Medora Stage and Forwarding Company," and that:

1. Our full and true names are Arthur T. Packard and Erasmus Deffebach.

2. That our residence is at the town of Medora, in the county of Billings, in the territory of Dakota.

3. That the principal place of business of said partnership is at the town of Medora aforesaid.

Dated, Medora, D. T., Sept. 8, 1884. ARTHUR T. PACKARD. ERASMUS DEFFEBACH. Witness: FRANK B. ALLEN.

TERRITORY OF DAKOTA, County of Billings, } ss.

On this eighth day of September, 1884, before me, Frank B. Allen, a notary public, personally appeared Arthur T. Packard and Erasmus Deffebach, to me well known as the same persons described in and who executed the foregoing instrument, and acknowledged that they executed the same freely and voluntarily for the uses and purposes therein expressed and specified.

In witness whereof I have hereunto set my hand and official seal at said county the day and year above written. [Seal] FRANK B. ALLEN, Notary Public.
articles.summary: Certificate filed under Dakota civil code: Arthur T. Packard and Erasmus Deffebach form the Medora Stage and Forwarding Company, dated Sept. 8, 1884, before notary Frank B. Allen.

articles.headline: Notice.
articles.text:
Notice.

We the undersigned, members of the Republican central committee of Billings county, having been petitioned by several representative voters of said county, hereby give notice that a mass Republican convention will be held at Belfied, Billings county, at the Riverside Hotel, on Saturday, October 11, 1884, at 7 o'clock p. m., for the purpose of electing two delegates to attend the legislative convention to be held at Bismarck, October 15, 1884.

This action is taken because the central committee of Billings county, as a body, has never been consulted, or a meeting called, on the subject of calling conventions, but instead of which the so-called chairman has assumed the responsibility of representing the voters of the county without having the authority to do so. GEO. BLANKENBERG, MAX BASS, Members of Central Committee.
articles.summary: Republican central committee members Geo. Blankenberg and Max Bass call a mass Republican convention at the Riverside Hotel, Belfield, for Oct. 11, 1884, to elect two delegates to the Bismarck legislative convention, accusing the county chairman of acting without authority.

articles.headline: Additional Local.
articles.text: A portion of the east wall of the church was blown down during the heavy wind storm Tuesday night.
articles.summary: An east wall section of the (Medora) church was blown down in Tuesday night's wind storm.

articles.text: The Marquis came up from St. Paul Monday evening in his special car. He will remain a few days.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès came up from St. Paul Monday evening in his special car and will stay a few days.

articles.text: Bob. Roberts' outfit will load with Black Hills freight to-morrow, consigned to Deadwood, Spearfish and Lead City merchants.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts' freighting outfit will load Black Hills freight for Deadwood, Spearfish and Lead City merchants.

articles.text: The plans of the new abattoir have arrived. Some alterations will be necessary, and we will not be able to publish a full description of the building until next week.
articles.summary: Plans for the new abattoir have arrived; alterations are needed and a full description is deferred a week.

articles.text: A. T. Packard, of the BAD LANDS COW BOY, General Manager of the Medora Stage Company, paid his devoirs to the Register yesterday, and to the G. A. R. ball last evening.—[Spearfish Register.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Spearfish Register noting a visit by A. T. Packard, general manager of the Medora Stage Company, and his attendance at the G. A. R. ball.

articles.text: Bob Roberts was compelled to shoot one of his bears this morning in order to relieve it from suffering, it having been wounded a few months ago by some unknown person who was indulging in promiscuous shooting.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts had to shoot one of his bears, wounded months earlier by a careless shooter.

articles.text:
The following very interesting communication was received by Mr. J. C. Fisher from a Bohemian friend in St. Paul:

DEAR FISHEROUSKY: Hgfvebnj knbsyk fud jnbutrk ewi opky yum. Bunxcf up oletzky to hell Ky nop dcxghq we rfv kokjui nb bnhj ynbhgf no goodde! T. J. KERR-OUSKY.

As no one could be found to translate the above it is supposed to be an application for a situation as stage driver on the Medora and Deadwood stage line.
articles.summary: A joke: a gibberish letter to J. C. Fisher from a 'Bohemian friend' in St. Paul, taken as an application to drive on the Medora-Deadwood stage line.

articles.text:
According to the time table which we publish this week the arrival and departure of stages will be as follows: The coaches will arrive Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays, at 6 p. m., connecting with westbound passenger train, and depart Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, at 8:30 a. m., connecting with eastbound train.

There will be five eating stations on the route, the outfits for which are on the ground ready for business. The stations as located are as follows: Medora, Davis creek, Rocky Ridge, Springdale, Buffalo creek, North Grand river, Cave Hills, Gallup's, Middle Grand river, South Grand, Macy's, Indian creek, DeMores, Spearfish, Deadwood.
articles.summary: Stage schedule for the Medora-Deadwood line and list of stations from Medora to Deadwood.

articles.text: Under the head "Center of Stockdom" a St. Paul paper states that the center of the cattle trade has moved north from Colorado, Nebraska and Wyoming to Montana and Dakota. Three cattle firms have 88,000 head on the Cheyenne, Belle Fourche and Little Missouri rivers. Altogether the Northern Pacific road has shipped this season over 2,000 cars of beeves, or 40,000 head from Montana to Chicago, and expects to ship 75,000 head before the close of the season. To the ranges in Montana and Western Dakota it has shipped 100,000 head of yearlings and two-year-olds this season from further east. The Powder River Cattle Co. has 60,000 head of cattle on its range, valued at $3,000,000, and has purchased lands at South Duluth on which cattle pens and yards will be built, where cattle may be kept until ready for shipment by boat to the east.
articles.summary: A St. Paul paper reports the center of the cattle trade moving north to Montana and Dakota, with three firms holding 88,000 head on the Cheyenne, Belle Fourche and Little Missouri rivers.

articles.headline: $250 REWARD.
articles.text:
STOCK NOTES.

$250 REWARD. The above reward will be paid for information leading to the arrest of any person or persons setting fire to the grass in the cattle sections of Western Dakota. N. P. REF. CAR CO. CONTINENTAL CATTLE CO. HUGHES & SIMPSON. DORR CLARK. CLARK & PLUM. DICKEY BROS. E. G. PADDOCK.
articles.summary: $250 reward offered by N. P. Ref. Car Co. and other ranchers for arrest of grass-fire setters in western Dakota.

articles.headline: $50 Reward.
articles.text:
$50 Reward. The above reward will be paid for the return of the following stock or a proportionate reward will be paid for the return of any of them. The stock consists of the following horses:

One bay mare, one brown mare and one roan mare, all young and branded double or reverse P on left shoulder as advertised in our brand columns. Also one light sorrel pony, white legs and face and branded NC on left shoulder and triangle JP on right shoulder also as advertised in our brand columns. GREGOR LANG, Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: Gregor Lang offers $50 reward for return of three mares and a sorrel pony.

articles.headline: Lost—$10 Reward.
articles.text: Lost—$10 Reward. Lost from the Little Missouri round-up, one bay horse 5 years old, branded J on left shoulder and S on right flank; partly broken and very wild when he left; had picket rope around neck. Any one returning or giving information of him will receive the above reward. W. N. THOMPSON & CO., Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: W. N. Thompson & Co. offer $10 for a bay horse lost from the Little Missouri round-up.

articles.text: Several cases of pleuro-pneumonia has been discovered in Illinois.
articles.summary: Pleuro-pneumonia found in Illinois.

articles.text: The Swan Land & Cattle Co., is now shipping from 1,000 to 1,200 beef steers per week to the Chicago market.
articles.summary: Swan Land & Cattle Co. shipping 1,000-1,200 beef steers weekly to Chicago.

articles.text: A Jersey cow at Hamilton, Ont, shows the unprecedented yield of thirty pounds and two ounces of butter in seven days.
articles.summary: Record butter yield from a Jersey cow at Hamilton, Ont.

articles.text: W. J. Pitney, of Augusta, Ill., has a grade Short-horn cow that gave birth to three healthy bull calves that are doing well.
articles.summary: Grade Short-horn cow of W. J. Pitney bears triplet bull calves.

articles.text: At a recent sale of Hamilton Short-horns at Flat Creek, Ky, fifty animals, several of them young calves, sold for $35,980, averaging $719,60.
articles.summary: Hamilton Short-horn sale at Flat Creek, Ky., brings $35,980.

articles.text: A Cattle train was wrecked on the Rock Island road Sept. 27. The fireman of the engine and a stockman were killed. A car of cattle were consumed by fire.
articles.summary: Cattle train wrecked on the Rock Island road Sept. 27; fireman and stockman killed.

articles.text: We hear of no new cases of Texas fever. The epidemic has probably disappeared for the present season. With proper precaution there need be no danger of its reappearance another year.
articles.summary: No new Texas fever cases reported.

articles.text: The cattle shipments from Dickinson last week were as follows: Continental Land and Cattle company, 140 cars; Clark & Plum, 16 cars; Dickey Bros., 105 cars. They were all consigned to Chicago.
articles.summary: Cattle shipped from Dickinson last week: Continental Land and Cattle Co. 140 cars, Clark & Plum 16, Dickey Bros. 105, all to Chicago.

articles.text: It is stated from all parts of the country that the cattle which a short time since were afflicted with sore eyes have recovered, and there is no new cases reported. The first frost removed the cause.
articles.summary: Sore-eye affliction among cattle cured by first frost.

articles.text: The Swan Land & Cattle Co. have 130,000 head of cattle in the Platte country and a capital of $3,375,000. They branded 20,000 calves this season and are shipping about twelve hundred head of beef steers per week.—[Yellowstone Journal.
articles.summary: Swan Land & Cattle Co.'s herd, capital and shipments (from Yellowstone Journal).

articles.text: At the great combination sale of Hereford cattle at Kansas City recently, Mr. Wm. Morgan, of Cheyenne, purchased "Primrose," the venerable mother of the Wyoming Hereford Association's famous bull "Rudolph," paying for the cow and her calf $1,500.
articles.summary: Wm. Morgan of Cheyenne buys Hereford cow 'Primrose' at Kansas City.

articles.text: Colorado last year had but 14,000 swine. The present year it will have 25,000. Ere two years more it will have 100,000. Prior to the present time the playful hog has cut but light caper in this country. In the future he will command respect.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Colorado's swine numbers growing.

articles.text: Those who give time, money and care to the breeding and feeding of scrub stock are, says an experienced breeder, beaten from the start. The same feed and care bestowed upon fine stock would yield a profit. Grade up by using full-blooded sires.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Breeder advises grading up with full-blooded sires.

articles.text: A fine herd of cattle were poisoned on John Watson's stock farm, twenty miles southwest of Morris, Minn., last Saturday, by drinking in an arm of the Pomme Deterre river, upon which a heavy green scum had collected. Twenty-six of the cattle are dead and others are expected to die.
articles.summary: Cattle poisoned on John Watson's farm near Morris, Minn.

articles.text: Miss Maud Reed, the cattle queen of the mountains, was drowned in the Grand river, a little below Grand Junction, a few days since. She was on her way to her cattle ranch on East creek, and while fording the river, in company with Coghill and Harry Taylor—two cattle men—were all swept down by the rushing waters and drowned.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Maud Reed, 'cattle queen of the mountains,' drowned in the Grand river with two cattlemen.

articles.text: The stockmen about Tombstone are excited, it seems. John Chisholm, a cattle king from Texas, is about to drive a large herd of cattle into Arizona. The stockmen of that section are aroused to the danger of being overshadowed by this cattle king, and if Chisholm moves in, they think they will have to move out, and they don't propose to do that without a struggle.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Tombstone stockmen alarmed that Texas cattle king John Chisholm will drive a large herd into Arizona (from N. M. Stock Grower).

articles.text: The sheep market is assuming a more cheerful look. In addition to an improved demand for shipment alive, one of our dressed meat concerns is now shipping an average of 400 carcasses per day. Prices have been discouragingly low all the season, and while there is no likelihood of any immediate decided advance, it is safe to conclude that the period of greatest depression has been passed.—[Breeder's Gazette
articles.summary: Sheep market improving (Breeder's Gazette).

articles.text: Wyoming has 800,000 head of cattle, valued at $30,000,000. Seven companies own one-third of all the cattle in the territory. Of the vast herds of cattle in Texas it is claimed that 1,000,000 head are owned by parties living outside of the state, and that a revenue of $10 per head is annually received by outsiders on these investments. Canadian exporters of beef have been heavy losers this season on their shipments to England. Many extensive shippers have gone out of the business.—[Chicago Commercial.
articles.summary: Wyoming and Texas cattle holdings and Canadian beef exporters' losses (Chicago Commercial).

articles.text: Monday's run of range cattle was in the neighborhood of 7,500 head—a considerably larger number than reported for any previous day of the season. This was followed Tuesday by 6,000 head, making nearly 14,000 head for the two days. The indications are that shipments from the plains have now begun in good earnest, and from this time on to the end of October average receipts of from 5,000 to 7,000 head per day may safely be counted on. Since Friday last there has been a decline in prices of 40@50c, and the market is still weak, with the chances in favor of a further shrinkage.—[Breeder's Gazette.
articles.summary: Heavy runs of range cattle at market; prices declining (Breeder's Gazette).

articles.text: A Montreal paper says: "Shippers of beef cattle from this point have been extraordinarily heavy losers this season. One firm shows a deficiency up to the present of $250,000. Another firm lost $150,000, and several from $50,000 to $150,000 each. The principal loss arises from purchasing before navigation, when prices were very high; and also in making contracts for freight throughout the season at increased rates over last year. The fall in prices in Great Britain made every consignment unprofitable. Over $3,000,000 worth of cattle have been shipped from here this season so far, the increase being great over last year.
articles.summary: Montreal beef cattle shippers' heavy losses.

articles.text: It is said that there are 15,000,000 horses in the United States, the average size of which has been in some way contributed to by the importations of Clydesdales and Normans. As, to keep up the supply, 1,000,000 must be bred annually, those who have made horse breeding for a foreign market their object, need not yet despair, though the demand may have fallen off. They have the best of Clydesdales, the best of Normans and a few Shires, but they need more of all; and the Cleveland blood much, as the best of the studs of the old Yorkshire breed out there has not been heavily touched. The Soffolks they do not seem inclined to recognize.—[English L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: U.S. horse numbers and breeding for foreign market (English L. S. Journal).

articles.text: Sidney Dillon, of world-wide fame as one of the Union Pacific potentates, is one of the heaviest cattle-owners in the Union. The firm of which he is the principal is known as Dillon & Co. Isaac Dillon constitutes the Co. He is the manager of the business, and lives on a ranch near North Platte. Their cattle are numbered by the thousand on a thousand hills. Some are in this valley and others up in the Snake River country. The headquarters cattle ranch, known as the "Stone ranch," is in the valley near O'Fallon's station and is surrounded by a splendid range, extending for many miles on the north and south. The able assistant to Mr. Dillon is Frank Alexander, than whom there is no better in the state.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Sidney Dillon's cattle operations near North Platte (Col. L. S. Record).

articles.text: For the last sixty days our receipts of cattle have been declining at the rate of fully one thousand head per day, as compared with the corresponding period last year. For this heavy loss it is not easy to fully account. A part of it may be ascribed to the late stringency in the money market, which made it difficult for intending shippers to get the usual bank accommodation, and a part may be charged to the cutting of rail freights by roads leading eastward from St. Louis and Kansas City, by which means a good deal of stock was diverted from this market; but the principal cause of the shortage is no doubt found in the almost certainty of a tremendous crop, all over the west, of corn and fodder. This led farmers to keep back thousands of young and unfinished cattle which with a less encouraging outlook would have been sent to market.—[Breeder's Gazette.
articles.summary: Declining cattle receipts explained by money market, freight cutting and big corn crop (Breeder's Gazette).

articles.text: Probably never before have the cattle raisers of the west been in better spirits than during the present season. Prices in some cases may not be quite so high at present, nor the profits be anything in excess of other years, but still there seems to prevail a good healthy feeling of satisfaction, all things considered. True the fall trade is attended with some drawbacks, as will always be the case in this or any other line of business, but up to date the receipts of cattle at Chicago and other points have been moderate, and this has had a tendency to keep the market steady. In no case have shippers been compelled to sell at losing figures on account of the market being glutted or over supplied, and if receipts at the market centres continue in the same moderate figures that have characterized them thus far, there can indeed be no cause for complaint.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Western cattle raisers in good spirits; markets steady (N. W. L. S. Journal).

articles.text: Stock Inspector Matthews was in town to-day.
articles.summary: Stock Inspector Matthews visited town.

articles.text: T. S. Houk, of Detroit, Mich., is visiting here.
articles.summary: T. S. Houk of Detroit visiting.

articles.text: Edward Rany, of Bismarck, was in town this week.
articles.summary: Edward Rany of Bismarck in town.

articles.text: Otto Fisher and Chas. Williams, of Bismarck, were in town last Friday.
articles.summary: Otto Fisher and Chas. Williams of Bismarck in town last Friday.

articles.text: The N. P. Ref. Car Co. will ship two carloads of sheep to Duluth this week.
articles.summary: N. P. Ref. Car Co. to ship two carloads of sheep to Duluth.

articles.text: Dr. D. M. McIntosh came down from Glendive yesterday on professional business.
articles.summary: Dr. D. M. McIntosh down from Glendive on professional business.

articles.text: J. R. Widmyer, of the Glendive Independent, made us a pleasant visit last Sunday.
articles.summary: J. R. Widmyer of the Glendive Independent visited the Cow Boy.

articles.text: Mr. C. L. Brinker, station agent at this place, is contemplating a visit to his home in Pennsylvania.
articles.summary: Station agent C. L. Brinker plans a visit home to Pennsylvania.

articles.text: J. A. Ferris' store not being adequate to hold his immense stock he has been compelled to build a large warehouse.
articles.summary: J. A. Ferris building a large warehouse for his store.

articles.text: Mr. A. T. Packard, editor of the COW BOY, is expected to return from the Hills on the first coach, which will arrive Tuesday evening.
articles.summary: Editor A. T. Packard expected back from the Black Hills on the first coach Tuesday evening.

articles.text: Passenger train No. 2 was thirteen hours late Tuesday. The delay was occasioned by a collision with a freight train on the Yellowstone division.
articles.summary: Passenger train No. 2 thirteen hours late Tuesday after a collision on the Yellowstone division.

articles.text: L. D. Pettit, of Belfield, stopped at Medora a short time this week en reute to Billings and other points in connection with his fast increasing bone business.
articles.summary: L. D. Pettit of Belfield passed through on bone-buying business.

articles.text: From five to ten trains of stock a day have been passing through Medora within the last few days. They are shipped from Miles City, Glendive and Mingusville.
articles.summary: Five to ten stock trains a day passing through Medora.

articles.text: J. Alden Eaton, manager of the Custer Trail Cattle company, and Mr. Stevenson, of Pittsburgh, Pa., who is visiting here, made the COW BOY office a pleasant call this morning.
articles.summary: J. Alden Eaton of the Custer Trail Cattle Co. and Mr. Stevenson of Pittsburgh called at the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: Bismarck will send two or three carloads of products of Burleigh county to the New Orleans exposition. It is expected that a total of twenty carloads will go from Dakota.
articles.summary: Bismarck to send carloads of Burleigh county products to the New Orleans exposition.

articles.text: D. H. Hostetter, of Pittsburgh, Pa., who has been visiting at Eaton' ranch for the past few weeks, started for home last Friday. Mr. Hostetter is the son of the celebrated Dr. Hostetter of bitters fame. Howard Eaton accompanied him east as far as Mandan.
articles.summary: D. H. Hostetter, son of the bitters maker, left the Eaton ranch for home; Howard Eaton went with him to Mandan.

articles.text: The Minnesela Boomer says "considerable freight now passes through Minnesela on its way from the Northern Pacific to the Hills, and it is only a question of a short time until nearly all the freight comes this way, as the road is being put in good shape.
articles.summary: Minnesela Boomer says Northern Pacific-to-Hills freight is going via Minnesela.

articles.text: Bob. Roberts, who is one of the deputy commissioners of Dakota for the New Orleans expositon, returned from Bismarck this week, where he had been in connection with his office. He has engaged Vic Smith to collect petrifactions and other curiosities for the exposition.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts, deputy commissioner for the New Orleans exposition, engaged Vic Smith to collect petrifactions and curiosities.

articles.text: Monday evening's westbound passenger train was delayed here about an hour and twenty minutes owing to one of the coaches running off the track while in the act of side-tracking the Marquis' special car. It seems that the track is in very poor condition, which alone caused the accident, no blame being attached to the train men.
articles.summary: Monday's westbound passenger was delayed 1 hr 20 min when a coach ran off the poor track while side-tracking the Marquis' special car.

articles.text: The following gentlemen have been invited to accompany the first stage to Deadwood, which leaves here next Monday morning, October 6: C. S. Fee, general passenger agent; J. M. Hanniford, general freight agent, and M. J. Hall, assistant superintendent N. P. express company, of St. Paul; Governor Pierce, Alex. McKenzie and F. B. Allen, of Bismarck.
articles.summary: Officials invited to ride the first stage to Deadwood Monday, Oct. 6.

articles.text: Mr Julius Lemoyne, of the Lemoyne Cattle company, who have their ranch on Tepee Bottom, arrived in Medora last Sunday evening. Mr Lemoyne's home is in Washington county, Pa., which is noted for its thoroughbred stock breeders, and is himself a breeder of thoroughbred Short-horn cattle and Berkshire swine. He is accompanied by Harry Kelly, of West Virginia, who is also interested in the breeding business.
articles.summary: Julius Lemoyne of the Lemoyne Cattle Co. (Tepee Bottom) arrived with Harry Kelly.

articles.text: The immigrant train last Tuesday had three carloads of Crow Indians aboard, who were in box cars and huddled together like so many cattle. They caused considerable amusement, as they were evidently hungry and commenced prying around the culinary departments of every hotel in town. They were gorgeously attired in various costumes and decorated with ornaments, paint, etc. They came from Fort Berthold, via Dickinson, and were en route to Fort Custer.
articles.summary: Three carloads of Crow Indians passed through on the immigrant train from Fort Berthold to Fort Custer.

articles.text: The Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan, was in town this week, and held mass Tuesday morning. He informed us that they were building a hospital at Mandan, called the Sisters' Hospital, which is 80x50 feet in dimension. It is to be a three-story brick building with Mansard roof. It is estimated that the cost of the building will be $25,000. In view of this fact he says all contributions will be gratefully received, and that he will soon give our citizens an opportunity to subscribe for this good cause as liberally as they wish. As this will be the only hospital between here and Brainerd it certainly is a much needed institution.
articles.summary: Father Martin of Mandan held mass in Medora and solicited support for the $25,000 Sisters' Hospital being built at Mandan.

articles.headline: Notice of Dissolution.
articles.text: Notice of Dissolution. MEDORA, September 18, 1884. Notice is hereby given that the firm of Coleman & Brown is this day mutually dissolved, M. M. Coleman continuing the business. All claims due and against the late firm must be settled by the said M. M. Coleman, unless fraudulently contracted. M. M. COLEMAN, C. F. BROWN. 33-4t
articles.summary: Coleman & Brown partnership at Medora dissolved Sept. 18, 1884; M. M. Coleman continues the business.
